newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary panel fails to agree EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary panel fails to agree EMU budget pact.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee made little progress on Tuesday towards agreement on a budget stability pact for countries joining a single currency.

EU monetary sources said the committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, will meet again next week to try to secure a final blueprint for a budget pact ahead of a summit of EU leaders next month in Dublin.
However, the sources said the most likely outcome would be a progress report with several important issues still outstanding.
"It remains to be seen what can be done, but I'm not that optimistic," said one source.

Tough German demands have so far blocked an accord on a pact that penalises governments running excessive deficits within a monetary union. It is considered by many to be an essential element of economic and monetary union (EMU).
Perhaps the toughest hurdle is agreement on a precise definition of a severe economic downturn which would let governments with deficits above three percent of gross domestic product avoid sanctions.

Germany very much wants a quantitative definition of what constitutes so-called "temporary and exceptional" circumstances. But others say a narrow definition of an economic recession is unrealistic given obvious differences among EU economies.
As a possible compromise, sources said the committe discussed the notion of a range, specifying the magnitude of negative growth a country must suffer if it is to avoid penalties.

The parameters were defined as negative growth of between 0.5 and 2.0 percent. If the decline in a country's total output fell within the specified range, a vote among EU finance ministers would be taken to determine whether it was an exceptional situation.
A qualified majority would be needed for such a verdict, which would then allow the country to avoid fines. If the decline in GDP was beyond the range, no vote would be needed.
It was unclear whether Germany would agree to such a proposal. Juergen Stark, state secretary for the German finance ministry, did not attend the meeting, sources added.
Stark was apparently present at a gathering of EU budget ministers which was held at the same time.
Apart from negotiations on the details of the stability pact, monetary officials say the EU's legislative process alone may preclude the possibility of an accord this year.
